newsitem.title: USA: W.House says budget will use CBO and OMB estimates.
newsitem.headline: W.House says budget will use CBO and OMB estimates.

text.p: U.S. Office of Management and Budget director Franklin Raines said Tuesday President Clinton's budget will show balance by 2002 regardless of whether the economic forecasts of the Congressional Budget Office or the White House are used.
The White House has said the fiscal 1998 budget, which is to be released Thursday, will contain projections showing a balanced budget by 2002.
"This budget is going to be balanced from birth to 2002," Raines told reporters after a meeting with Democratic senators.

Raines, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles briefed the senators on the coming budget and discussed administration objections to the proposed balanced budget constitutional amendment.
The nonpartisan CBO's economic forecasts have generally been more conservative on future economic growth than those produced by the White House's OMB.
Sen. Joseph Lieberman, Democrat of Connecticut, told reporters that the White House team said economic forecasts used to estimate the budget would be "conservative."
The CBO in December forecast real GDP for calendar 1998 at 2.0 percent and the agency's estimates in previous years have generally been slightly lower than White House forecasts.

The Senate Budget Committee's senior Democrat, Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, said the White House tax plan was generally as reported. "They're holding to what is common knowledge and that is the ... targeted capital gains, education credits and deductions are pretty much as a package about $100 billion, offset by approximately half of that."

The Senate Finance Committee Wednesday is to vote on a proposed one-year extension of the airport trust fund excise tax which expired in December 1996. The airline ticket tax is expected to be included in Clinton's budget.

Maryland Sen. Paul Sarbanes said Rubin's presented administration views on the balanced budget amendment that paralleled testimony Rubin has given Congress. Rubin has warned it would jeopardize Social Security in the next century and could worsen any economic downturn if Washington is prevented from responding with tax cuts or spending to mitigate a recession.
Of Democrats who voted for the amendment last year, Sen. Joseph Biden of Delaware said he was hoping for changes to meet his concerns that a 3/5 vote be needed to raise taxes.
